section: CLASSIFICATION, groups subordinate to groups
label: Descent with divergence and extinction produces groups subordinate to groups
claim: The nested arrangement of organisms into groups within groups (species within genera, genera within families, and so on) results from the modified descendants of a single progenitor diverging in character while less divergent forms are exterminated.
quote: he will see that the inevitable result is that the modified descendants proceeding from one progenitor become broken up into groups subordinate to groups.
scope: all organic beings, living and extinct
measurable_quantities: degree of hierarchical (tree-like) structure in character or sequence data
consistency of nested clades across independent character sets
candidate_data: Large phylogenies and their underlying character and sequence matrices (Open Tree of Life, GenBank, TreeBASE) allow tests of how tree-like the pattern of similarity is.

section: Natural system
label: The Natural System expresses propinquity of descent
claim: The 'something more' than mere resemblance that naturalists seek in the Natural System is closeness of descent, which is the only known cause of similarity among organisms and is partially revealed by classifications.
quote: propinquity of descent,—the only known cause of the similarity of organic beings,—is the bond, hidden as it is by various degrees of modification, which is partially revealed to us by our classifications.
scope: biological classification of all organisms
measurable_quantities: congruence between traditional morphology-based classifications and independently inferred phylogenies
candidate_data: Comparison of traditional Linnaean taxonomies (e.g. Catalogue of Life, GBIF backbone) with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
label: Characters least modified by adaptation are most constant and useful in classification
claim: The value of a character for classification depends on its constancy across large groups of species, and characters are constant when they have been little changed in adapting species to their conditions of life; hence parts least concerned with special habits are generally the most useful for classification.
quote: But their importance for classification, I believe, depends on their greater constancy throughout large groups of species; and this constancy depends on such organs having generally been subjected to less change in the adaptation of the species to their conditions of life.
scope: characters of animals and plants used in systematics
measurable_quantities: homoplasy or consistency index of characters
association between a character's ecological/functional relevance and its homoplasy
candidate_data: Published morphological character matrices (MorphoBank, TreeBASE) analysed on reference phylogenies to compare homoplasy of habit-related versus other characters.

section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
label: Branches equally related by descent can differ greatly in amount of modification
claim: A natural arrangement of groups must be strictly genealogical, but branches that are equally closely related to a common progenitor may differ greatly in how much they have been modified, and these differing amounts of difference are what is expressed by ranking them as different genera, families or orders.
quote: I believe that the _arrangement_ of the groups within each class, in due subordination and relation to the other groups, must be strictly genealogical in order to be natural; but that the _amount_ of difference in the several branches or groups, though allied in the same degree in blood to their common progenitor, may differ greatly, being due to the different degrees of modification which they have undergone
scope: all classes of organisms
measurable_quantities: morphological disparity or rate of change among sister lineages of equal age
variation in evolutionary rates among lineages
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with morphological matrices (MorphoBank) to compare rates of morphological change across sister clades.

section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
label: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary
claim: The relative value of groups such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families and genera is, at least at present, almost arbitrary, as shown by groups being raised in rank merely because more allied species were discovered.
quote: Finally, with respect to the comparative value of the various groups of species, such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families, and genera, they seem to be, at least at present, almost arbitrary.
scope: taxonomic ranks above the species level
measurable_quantities: variation in crown or stem age of taxa of the same rank
variation in species richness and disparity among taxa of the same rank
candidate_data: Divergence times of genera, families and orders across groups from TimeTree, with taxonomy from the Catalogue of Life or GBIF backbone.

section: Classification of varieties
label: Varieties form nested groups for the same reason species do
claim: Domestic and natural varieties fall into groups subordinate to groups (sub-varieties under varieties under species) for the same reason species do, namely closeness of descent combined with various degrees of modification.
quote: The origin of the existence of groups subordinate to groups, is the same with varieties as with species, namely, closeness of descent with various degrees of modification.
scope: varieties and breeds of domestic and wild species
measurable_quantities: hierarchical clustering of breeds or varieties
agreement between breed clustering and documented breed histories
candidate_data: Genome-wide population data for domestic breeds (e.g. dog, pigeon, cattle and chicken breed panels in GenBank/SRA) compared with recorded breed pedigrees.

section: Descent always used in classification
label: Characters shared across species with very different habits indicate common inheritance
claim: However trifling a character, if it occurs throughout many species with very different habits of life it can be explained only by inheritance from a common parent, and so has high value for classification; for the same reason rudimentary structures can be as useful as other parts.
quote: if it prevail throughout many and different species, especially those having very different habits of life, it assumes high value; for we can account for its presence in so many forms with such different habits, only by its inheritance from a common parent.
scope: characters of animals and plants within large groups
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic signal of characters
fit of character distributions to a single origin versus multiple origins
candidate_data: Trait datasets mapped onto phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TreeBASE, MorphoBank) to estimate the number of origins of widely shared characters.

section: Analogical or adaptive characters
label: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form
claim: Animals from very distinct lines of descent can become adapted to similar conditions and so acquire a close external resemblance; such analogical or adaptive resemblances conceal rather than reveal blood-relationship, so they are almost worthless for classification between groups, although the same characters can indicate true affinity within a group.
quote: For animals, belonging to two most distinct lines of descent, may readily become adapted to similar conditions, and thus assume a close external resemblance; but such resemblances will not reveal—will rather tend to conceal their blood-relationship to their proper lines of descent.
scope: animals (and plants) of distinct lineages living under similar conditions
measurable_quantities: frequency of convergent morphological evolution
mismatch between morphology-based groupings and phylogeny for habit-related traits
candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life combined with ecomorphological trait data (e.g. AVONET for birds, PanTHERIA for mammals) to quantify convergence among unrelated lineages.

section: CLASSIFICATION, groups subordinate to groups
label: Expanding dominant groups explain why all life falls into a few great classes
claim: Larger and more dominant groups tend to keep increasing in size and to supplant smaller, feebler groups, which is why all organisms, recent and extinct, fall into a few great orders, still fewer classes, and a single natural system.
quote: The larger and more dominant groups thus tend to go on increasing in size; and they consequently supplant many smaller and feebler groups. Thus we can account for the fact that all organisms, recent and extinct, are included under a few great orders, under still fewer classes, and all in one great natural system.
scope: all higher taxa through geological time
measurable_quantities: relationship between clade size and subsequent diversification rate
clade extinction rate as a function of clade size
candidate_data: Fossil occurrence data from the Paleobiology Database and dated molecular phylogenies (TimeTree) to test whether large clades grow and small clades disappear.

section: Affinities, general, complex and radiating
label: Aberrant groups are species-poor relicts of extinction
claim: Aberrant or osculant groups are the surviving remnants of failing groups that suffered heavy extinction; consequently they are generally represented by very few species, and those species are usually very distinct from each other.
quote: And we have some evidence of aberrant forms having suffered severely from extinction, for they are generally represented by extremely few species; and such species as do occur are generally very distinct from each other, which again implies extinction.
scope: aberrant (phylogenetically isolated) genera and higher groups
measurable_quantities: species richness of phylogenetically isolated lineages
branch length or evolutionary distinctiveness
fossil diversity history of relict clades
candidate_data: Evolutionary-distinctiveness scores computed on large phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) compared with clade species richness, plus Paleobiology Database records of past diversity of relict clades.

section: Affinities, general, complex and radiating
label: Affinities of one group to another are usually general, not to any single species
claim: When a member of one group shows a real affinity to a quite distinct group, the affinity is usually general rather than to any particular species, because it retains characters of an ancient common progenitor of both groups.
quote: when a member belonging to one group of animals exhibits an affinity to a quite distinct group, this affinity in most cases is general and not special
scope: members of distinct orders or families of animals and plants that show cross-group affinities
measurable_quantities: similarity of a taxon to each member of another group
phylogenetic position of taxa showing cross-group affinity (near the base of their group or not)
candidate_data: Morphological matrices (MorphoBank) and phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) to test whether taxa with cross-group affinities are early-diverging lineages.

section: Extinction separates and defines groups
label: Gaps between groups, even whole classes, are due to extinction of connecting forms
claim: Extinction has defined and widened the intervals between groups; even the distinctness of whole classes, such as birds from other vertebrates, results from the loss of many ancient forms that once connected their early progenitors.
quote: We may thus account even for the distinctness of whole classes from each other—for instance, of birds from all other vertebrate animals—by the belief that many ancient forms of life have been utterly lost, through which the early progenitors of birds were formerly connected with the early progenitors of the other vertebrate classes.
scope: classes and other higher groups, especially vertebrate classes
measurable_quantities: occurrence of fossil forms intermediate between currently distinct classes
morphological gap between groups before and after including fossil taxa
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences and published fossil character matrices (MorphoBank), e.g. for the dinosaur-to-bird transition.

section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
label: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions
claim: Within a class, homologous parts may change to almost any extent in form and size but always remain connected in the same order; for example, the bones of the arm and forearm are never transposed.
quote: the parts may change to almost any extent in form and size, and yet they always remain connected together in the same order.
scope: homologous structures within classes (vertebrate limbs, insect mouthparts, crustacean limbs, flowers)
measurable_quantities: frequency of changes in topological connectivity of homologous elements versus changes in shape and size
candidate_data: Comparative anatomical datasets and ontologies (e.g. Uberon, MorphoBank matrices) recording element connectivity across taxa.

section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
label: Unity of type reflects a common progenitor's pattern modified by slight steps
claim: The shared pattern of homologous organs within a class is explained by descent from an ancient progenitor (an archetype) that already had that pattern, which natural selection then modified by slight successive steps for different uses without transposing parts.
quote: If we suppose that the ancient progenitor, the archetype as it may be called, of all mammals, had its limbs constructed on the existing general pattern, for whatever purpose they served, we can at once perceive the plain signification of the homologous construction of the limbs throughout the whole class.
scope: members of the same class (e.g. mammal limbs, insect mouthparts)
measurable_quantities: presence of the shared pattern in early fossil members of the class
reconstructed ancestral states of homologous structures
candidate_data: Fossil occurrence and morphology data (Paleobiology Database, MorphoBank) for early members of classes, with ancestral-state reconstruction on Open Tree of Life phylogenies.

section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
label: Serially homologous parts derive from many repeated similar elements in progenitors
claim: Serial homologies within one individual (skull and vertebrae, jaws and legs of crustaceans, floral parts and leaves) arise because the progenitors of vertebrates, articulates and flowering plants had many repeated similar parts, which natural selection adapted to diverse purposes while inheritance retained a fundamental resemblance.
quote: An indefinite repetition of the same part or organ is the common characteristic (as Owen has observed) of all low or little-modified forms; therefore we may readily believe that the unknown progenitor of the vertebrata possessed many vertebræ; the unknown progenitor of the articulata, many segments; and the unknown progenitor of flowering plants, many spiral whorls of leaves.
scope: vertebrates, articulates (arthropods and annelids) and flowering plants
measurable_quantities: number and similarity of serially repeated elements in early fossil members versus later members of each group
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences and fossil morphological matrices (MorphoBank) for early arthropods, vertebrates and seed plants.

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Embryos of different animals in the same class are strikingly similar
claim: Embryos of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar, more so than the adults, and the points of resemblance often have no direct relation to their conditions of existence.
quote: The embryos, also, of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar
scope: animals within the same class, especially vertebrates and insects
measurable_quantities: morphological similarity of embryos across species by developmental stage
embryonic versus adult between-species divergence
candidate_data: Comparative embryo image and staging collections and published cross-species developmental time series (morphological and transcriptomic) for vertebrates and insects.

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Active larvae are adapted to their own conditions as fully as adults
claim: Whenever an embryo or larva becomes active and must provide for itself, it is as perfectly adapted to its conditions of life as the adult, and such adaptations can make the larvae of allied species differ as much as or more than their adults, though most larvae still follow the law of embryonic resemblance.
quote: The period of activity may come on earlier or later in life; but whenever it comes on, the adaptation of the larva to its conditions of life is just as perfect and as beautiful as in the adult animal.
scope: animals with free-living larval stages (e.g. insects, crustaceans, cirripedes)
measurable_quantities: larval versus adult morphological divergence among allied species
association between larval ecology and larval morphology
candidate_data: Comparative larval and adult morphological datasets for marine invertebrates and insects mapped on phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Embryological facts follow from late-appearing variations inherited at corresponding ages
claim: The leading facts of embryology are explained because, in the descendants of a common progenitor, successive slight modifications generally do not appear at a very early period of life (though they may be caused earlier) and are inherited at a corresponding later age, leaving embryos little modified.
quote: the leading facts in embryology, which are second in importance to none in natural history, are explained on the principle of slight modifications not appearing, in the many descendants from some one ancient progenitor, at a very early period in the life of each, though perhaps caused at the earliest, and being inherited at a corresponding not early period.
scope: animals generally
measurable_quantities: developmental stage at which between-species differences first appear
divergence of developmental trajectories across ontogeny
candidate_data: Comparative ontogenetic morphometric series and cross-species developmental time series for vertebrates and insects.

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Young of domestic breeds differ much less than adults
claim: The characteristic differences between domestic breeds produced by man's selection (in dogs, horses and pigeons) generally do not appear early in life and are inherited at a corresponding later age, so that the young of different breeds differ far less in proportions than the adults, with occasional exceptions such as the short-faced tumbler pigeon.
quote: the characteristic differences which give value to each breed, and which have been accumulated by man’s selection, have not generally first appeared at an early period of life, and have been inherited by the offspring at a corresponding not early period.
scope: domestic breeds of dogs, horses and pigeons
measurable_quantities: proportional differences between breeds at hatching or birth versus adulthood
ontogenetic allometric trajectories by breed
candidate_data: Published ontogenetic morphometric data for dog and pigeon breeds (e.g. skull growth series in museum collections and Dryad datasets).

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Community of embryonic structure reveals community of descent
claim: Because the embryo is the animal in a less modified state that partly reveals the structure of its progenitor, two groups that pass through the same or similar embryonic stages are descended from the same or similar parents, however different their adults; this is why embryonic characters are the most valuable for classification.
quote: Thus, community in embryonic structure reveals community of descent.
scope: animal groups, e.g. cirripedes recognised as crustaceans by their larvae
measurable_quantities: agreement between groupings based on embryonic/larval characters and independent phylogenies
agreement between adult-character groupings and independent phylogenies
candidate_data: Larval and adult morphological matrices (MorphoBank) compared against molecular phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, GenBank).

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Ancient extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants
claim: Since embryos partly show the structure of less modified ancient progenitors, ancient and extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants, though this may be obscured by early-appearing variations and may be undemonstrable because the geological record does not reach back far enough.
quote: we can clearly see why ancient and extinct forms of life should resemble the embryos of their descendants,—our existing species.
scope: extinct ancestors and the embryos of their living descendants
measurable_quantities: similarity of fossil adult morphology to embryonic versus adult morphology of living relatives
candidate_data: Fossil morphological data (Paleobiology Database, MorphoBank) combined with ontogenetic series of living relatives.

section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
label: Rudimentary organs are extremely common throughout nature
claim: Rudimentary, atrophied or aborted organs that bear the stamp of uselessness are extremely common in animals and plants.
quote: Organs or parts in this strange condition, bearing the stamp of inutility, are extremely common throughout nature.
scope: animals and plants generally
measurable_quantities: proportion of taxa possessing vestigial structures
number of documented vestigial structures per clade
candidate_data: Comparative anatomical databases and ontologies (e.g. Uberon, Phenoscape) annotated for reduced or vestigial structures.

section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
label: Rudimentary organs are highly variable
claim: Rudimentary organs vary greatly in development among individuals of the same species, and the degree of reduction of the same organ can differ much between closely allied species; because they are useless, their variations are not checked by natural selection.
quote: Rudimentary organs in the individuals of the same species are very liable to vary in degree of development and in other respects.
scope: rudimentary organs in animals and plants
measurable_quantities: within-species coefficient of variation of vestigial versus functional structures
candidate_data: Morphometric data on vestigial structures (e.g. cave-fish eyes, flightless-bird wings) in museum collections and Dryad datasets.

section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
label: Rudimentary organs are relatively larger in the embryo than in the adult
claim: As a universal rule, a rudimentary part is relatively larger compared with adjoining parts in the embryo than in the adult, and some rudiments (such as the teeth of whales and ruminants) appear in the embryo and then wholly disappear.
quote: It is also, I believe, a universal rule, that a rudimentary part or organ is of greater size relatively to the adjoining parts in the embryo, than in the adult
scope: rudimentary organs in animals and plants
measurable_quantities: relative size of rudimentary organs across ontogenetic stages
candidate_data: Ontogenetic series and embryological descriptions of vestigial structures (e.g. whale and ruminant tooth germs, snake limb buds) in museum collections and literature.

section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
label: Disuse is the main cause of rudimentary organs
claim: Disuse over successive generations has been the main agency reducing organs to rudiments (as with eyes of cave animals and wings of island birds), aided by natural selection where an organ becomes injurious; because reduction occurs at maturity and is inherited at a corresponding age, rudiments remain relatively larger in the embryo.
quote: I believe that disuse has been the main agency; that it has led in successive generations to the gradual reduction of various organs, until they have become rudimentary
scope: organs reduced under changed habits or conditions, e.g. cave animals and island birds
measurable_quantities: degree of organ reduction versus time since habitat change
evidence of reduction under relaxed versus active selection
candidate_data: Studies of cave-fish (Astyanax) and island flightless birds with dated phylogenies (TimeTree), plus experimental-evolution datasets in Dryad.

section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
label: Descent with modification embraces all members of each class
claim: Because all members of whole classes are linked by chains of affinities, fossils fill wide gaps between orders, rudiments imply fully developed ancestral organs, and structures within a class share one pattern and similar embryos, descent with modification embraces all members of the same class.
quote: Therefore I cannot doubt that the theory of descent with modification embraces all the members of the same class.
scope: all members of each class of animals and plants
measurable_quantities: monophyly of classes in independent phylogenies
support for common ancestry within each class
candidate_data: Phylogenomic datasets and synthetic trees (Open Tree of Life, GenBank/SRA) testing monophyly and common ancestry of classes.

section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
label: Animals from at most four or five progenitors, plants from as many or fewer
claim: All animals have descended from at most four or five progenitors, and all plants from an equal or smaller number.
quote: I believe that animals have descended from at most only four or five progenitors, and plants from an equal or lesser number.
scope: all animals and all plants
measurable_quantities: number of independent origins of animals and of plants inferred from phylogenetic data
candidate_data: Phylogenomic data for animals and plants (GenBank/SRA, Open Tree of Life) testing monophyly of each kingdom versus multiple independent origins.

section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
label: All living things share chemical composition, cell structure and laws of growth
claim: All living things have much in common in their chemical composition, germinal vesicles, cellular structure, and laws of growth and reproduction, as shown even by the same poison often affecting plants and animals similarly.
quote: Nevertheless all living things have much in common, in their chemical composition, their germinal vesicles, their cellular structure, and their laws of growth and reproduction.
scope: all living organisms
measurable_quantities: shared biochemical components and pathways across kingdoms
shared cellular structures across kingdoms
candidate_data: Cross-kingdom biochemical pathway and protein databases (KEGG, UniProt) documenting shared metabolism and cell components.

section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
label: Probably all organisms descend from one primordial form
claim: By analogy, probably all organisms that have ever lived on earth have descended from a single primordial form.
quote: Therefore I should infer from analogy that probably all the organic beings which have ever lived on this earth have descended from some one primordial form, into which life was first breathed.
scope: all organisms that have ever lived on earth
measurable_quantities: statistical support for universal common ancestry versus multiple independent origins
candidate_data: Universally conserved sequence data (e.g. ribosomal RNA and protein sequences in GenBank, SILVA) used in formal tests of universal common ancestry.

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Species differ from varieties only in their intermediates having existed formerly
claim: The only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is that varieties are known or believed to be connected by intermediate gradations at present, whereas species were connected by them in the past; species should therefore be treated, like genera, as combinations made for convenience.
quote: Hereafter we shall be compelled to acknowledge that the only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is, that the latter are known, or believed, to be connected at the present day by intermediate gradations, whereas species were formerly thus connected.
scope: species and varieties of all organisms
candidate_data: none known

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Organism-to-organism relations are the most important cause of organic change
claim: The most important cause of organic change is the mutual relation of organism to organism, in which the improvement of one form causes the improvement or extermination of others; this is almost independent of changes, even sudden ones, in physical conditions.
quote: the most important of all causes of organic change is one which is almost independent of altered and perhaps suddenly altered physical conditions, namely, the mutual relation of organism to organism,—the improvement of one being entailing the improvement or the extermination of others
scope: all organisms over geological time
measurable_quantities: relative explanatory power of biotic interactions (diversity, competitors) versus abiotic change (climate, sea level) for origination and extinction rates
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data analysed together with paleoclimate and sea-level records.

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Amount of fossil change between formations measures elapsed time
claim: Because species are produced and exterminated by slow, still-acting causes, the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations is probably a fair, though imperfect, measure of the time elapsed, and can be used to estimate the length of the blank intervals between formations.
quote: it follows, that the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations probably serves as a fair measure of the lapse of actual time.
scope: fossil faunas and floras of successive formations
measurable_quantities: faunal turnover between successive units
radiometrically dated time intervals between units
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences with ages from the Geologic Time Scale to correlate taxonomic turnover with absolute elapsed time.

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Rate of organic change was slower early in life's history
claim: In early periods of earth's history, when forms of life were fewer and simpler, the rate of organic change was probably slower, and at the first dawn of life it may have been extremely slow.
quote: During early periods of the earth’s history, when the forms of life were probably fewer and simpler, the rate of change was probably slower; and at the first dawn of life, when very few forms of the simplest structure existed, the rate of change may have been slow in an extreme degree.
scope: life on earth across its whole history
measurable_quantities: origination and extinction rates through time
rates of morphological change in early versus later clades
relationship between standing diversity and rate of change
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database diversity and turnover curves through the Phanerozoic, plus Precambrian microfossil and dated-phylogeny data (TimeTree).

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Known geological history is a fragment of the time since the first organism
claim: The whole history of the world as known from geology is only a small fragment of the time that has elapsed since the first organism, the progenitor of all later forms, came into existence.
quote: The whole history of the world, as at present known, although of a length quite incomprehensible by us, will hereafter be recognised as a mere fragment of time, compared with the ages which have elapsed since the first creature, the progenitor of innumerable extinct and living descendants, was created.
scope: history of life on earth
measurable_quantities: age of the earliest evidence of life
age of the base of the Silurian/Cambrian fossil record
candidate_data: Radiometric ages from the Geologic Time Scale, Precambrian fossil records (Paleobiology Database) and molecular-clock estimates (TimeTree).

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Every mental power was acquired by gradation
claim: Each mental power and capacity must have been acquired gradually, so psychology will rest on this foundation, and light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history.
quote: Psychology will be based on a new foundation, that of the necessary acquirement of each mental power and capacity by gradation.
scope: mental powers of animals, including man
measurable_quantities: distribution of cognitive abilities across related species
phylogenetic signal in cognitive traits
candidate_data: Comparative cognition datasets across primates and other animals (e.g. ManyPrimates), mapped on Open Tree of Life phylogenies.

section: Concluding remarks
label: Few living species will leave descendants; common species of dominant groups will prevail
claim: Very few living species will leave descendants in the far future, and those that will prevail and give rise to new dominant species will be the common, widespread species of the larger, dominant groups.
quote: We can so far take a prophetic glance into futurity as to foretel that it will be the common and widely-spread species, belonging to the larger and dominant groups, which will ultimately prevail and procreate new and dominant species.
scope: living species and their future descendants (testable retrospectively in the fossil record)
measurable_quantities: survival and origination probability versus geographic range size and abundance
survival versus size of the higher group
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data to relate past range size and clade size to lineage survival and production of daughter taxa.

section: Concluding remarks
label: Succession by generation has never been broken by a world-wide cataclysm
claim: Since all living forms are lineal descendants of forms that lived long before the Silurian epoch, the ordinary succession by generation has never once been broken and no cataclysm has ever desolated the whole world.
quote: As all the living forms of life are the lineal descendants of those which lived long before the Silurian epoch, we may feel certain that the ordinary succession by generation has never once been broken, and that no cataclysm has desolated the whole world.
scope: the history of life on earth
measurable_quantities: continuity of lineages across mass-extinction boundaries
proportion of lineages surviving each extinction event
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database records across mass-extinction boundaries and dated phylogenies (TimeTree) showing lineages crossing them.

section: Concluding remarks
label: Natural selection makes endowments tend towards perfection
claim: Because natural selection works solely by and for the good of each being, all bodily and mental endowments will tend to progress towards perfection.
quote: And as natural selection works solely by and for the good of each being, all corporeal and mental endowments will tend to progress towards perfection.
scope: all organisms over long periods
measurable_quantities: long-term trends in measures of adaptation or fitness
candidate_data: Long-term experimental evolution of fitness (LTEE) and long-run fossil trends in the Paleobiology Database bear on part of the claim.

section: Concluding remarks
label: The 'entangled bank' laws produce the diversity of living forms
claim: The varied and interdependent forms of life were produced by laws still acting: growth with reproduction; inheritance; variability caused by external conditions and by use and disuse; a rate of increase high enough to cause a struggle for life and so natural selection, which in turn causes divergence of character and extinction of less improved forms.
quote: These laws, taken in the largest sense, being Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance which is almost implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and direct action of the external conditions of life, and from use and disuse; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved forms.
scope: all organic beings
measurable_quantities: heritability of traits
standing variation
reproductive excess and mortality
selection differentials
rates of divergence and extinction
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution datasets (LTEE, Dryad), long-term wild-population studies, and Paleobiology Database diversification data each address components of the claim.
